# Appeal of Denial — Partial Knee Replacement (CPT 27446)

**Policy:** Aetna CPB 0660 – Knee Arthroplasty (https://www.aetna.com/cpb/medical/data/600_699/0660.html; last review 02/26/2026)

**Member:** Quinn Ellison
**Member ID:** W391580594
**Denial date:** 2026-08-04
**Reference number:** POC-DF42BEB029-97975
**Payer/Plan:** Aetna (Commercial/ACA), Montana

Dear Aetna Appeals Department,

I am appealing the denial of my prior authorization request for a partial knee replacement (CPT 27446). My surgeon, Dr. Lindqvist, has documented that this procedure is medically necessary, and I am asking Aetna to reconsider this decision.

The denial notice states that "the imaging findings submitted do not support the medical necessity of the requested procedure." I believe this conclusion does not match Aetna's own published criteria in CPB 0660, or the records already in my file.

**1. The imaging shows a single-compartment problem, which is exactly what this procedure is for.**

Aetna's policy states that "unicompartmental knee arthroplasty (UKA) is indicated when only 1 compartment is affected, and total knee arthroplasty (TKA) is indicated when 2 or 3 compartments are affected." My MRI from 2026-05-28 shows full-thickness cartilage loss and bone-on-bone apposition in the medial compartment only, with Kellgren-Lawrence grade 4 changes medially. Nothing in the imaging or exam findings describes involvement of the lateral or patellofemoral compartments. This is a single-compartment finding, which is the situation the policy describes as appropriate for UKA rather than TKA.

The policy also states that "Unicompartmental knee arthroplasty using Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved devices is considered medically necessary for members with advanced osteoarthritis or post-traumatic arthritis of the knee affecting only a single compartment (medial, lateral or patellofemoral), and who meet the following criteria." My diagnosis is advanced osteoarthritis limited to the medial compartment, which fits the condition this section addresses.

**2. I have completed the conservative treatment the policy asks for.**

The policy states that members "should have at least 12 weeks of non-surgical treatment documented in the medical record (at least 24 weeks for persons with a relative contraindication) - with at least half of the necessary conservative therapy consisting of formal physical therapy (in-person with a licensed physical therapist as opposed to home or virtual physical therapy) in the past year." My record shows 16 weeks of supervised, in-person physical therapy (24 visits, 2026-02-25 to 2026-06-17), documented in the physical therapy discharge note, along with 8 months of NSAID use and a corticosteroid injection on 2026-05-02. This exceeds the 12-week threshold and satisfies the requirement that at least half of the treatment be formal, in-person physical therapy.

The policy also lists "History of unsuccessful conservative therapy (non-surgical medical management" as part of the medical necessity criteria. My records document that NSAIDs gave inadequate relief over 8 months, and the corticosteroid injection gave only about 4 weeks of partial relief. My pain has continued for 18 months, I cannot climb stairs without assistance, and I wake 3-4 times nightly from pain. This shows that conservative therapy was tried in good faith and did not resolve my symptoms.

**3. My condition matches what the policy describes as severe enough that further conservative care may not be reasonable.**

The policy notes that "Conservative therapy may be inappropriate for severe osteoarthritis with bone-on-bone articulation in the weight-bearing portion of the joint (medial and/or lateral but not patello-femoral) or severe angular deformity." My MRI documents bone-on-bone apposition in the medial, weight-bearing compartment. This is the specific finding the policy identifies as a situation where continuing conservative treatment may not be a reasonable path forward — even though, in my case, I still completed 16 weeks of supervised physical therapy plus medication and injection therapy before requesting surgery.

**4. I do not have the contraindications the policy describes.**

The policy states that "Total joint replacement is considered not medically necessary in persons with any of the following absolute contraindications." My records show no active infection and no untreated substance use, which are the type of concerns this section of the policy addresses.

Given this, I do not understand how the stated reason for denial — that the imaging does not support medical necessity — is consistent with the plan's own criteria. My MRI shows the exact single-compartment finding the policy uses to distinguish UKA from TKA, and my chart documents conservative therapy well beyond the 12-week minimum.

**I am requesting that Aetna reverse this denial and approve the partial knee replacement (CPT 27446) as requested by Dr. Lindqvist.**

I understand this appeal must be received by 2027-01-31, and I am submitting it well before that date. I will complete Aetna's Member Complaint and Appeal Form, available in my account at aetna.com under complaints, grievances and appeals, and will fax or mail it to the address printed on my denial letter, which I am confirming before sending. I understand I can also reach Aetna by fax at 859-425-3379 or by phone at 1-800-872-3862 or the number on my member card.

Please let me know if any additional records from Dr. Lindqvist or my physical therapy provider would help with this review.

Thank you for reconsidering my request.

Sincerely,

Quinn Ellison
Member ID: W391580594
[Address]
[Phone number]
[Email address]
[Date]

---

*This letter is not medical or legal advice and does not guarantee that coverage will be approved.*
